compare_blocks.body:

compare_blocks.body:
The following fictional examples show how people might handle the same information. Either type can do any of the tasks. Assign work according to experience, access, authority and availability.

Before the stream, agree on who can answer a question, which facts can be shared and who will follow up if an answer is unavailable.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: a cousin asks about three cameras

In a fictional example, a cousin who wants to start making videos shares the same budget, list of three cameras and specification sheet with two relatives. Both have the same information about how the camera will be used.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: when a livestream loses its connection

In a fictional livestream, the connection drops forty minutes in. Both colleagues can see the same status information and use the same approved alert and backup options. Neither yet knows when the stream will return.

One useful contribution is an audience update stating what is known and when the team will update them again. Another is checking the approved backup and recording what is still uncertain. Either colleague can take either task if they have authority.

If the team knows the next update time, it can share that without promising when service will resume. The choice to post or check the backup depends on the information and assignments, so it cannot identify a type.

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two colleagues on a live production team who both check a product record before answering a question. A shared preference for concrete evidence could fit that choice, and so could a team procedure. The action alone gives little evidence about either type.

Both profiles have S, the preference for concrete details and experience. Type dynamics gives ESFJ introverted Sensing (Si) and ISTP extraverted Sensing (Se) as auxiliary functions. Neither limits a person to what is visible right now.

E/I concerns where attention goes. T/F concerns what carries weight in a decision. J/P concerns how much to settle in the outside world. A person can discuss a question with others, apply a rule consistently and still keep more than one option open.

The following fictional examples show how people might handle the same information. Either type can do any of the tasks. Assign work according to experience, access, authority and availability.

Before the stream, agree on who can answer a question, which facts can be shared and who will follow up if an answer is unavailable.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: an upset viewer reports a faulty product

In a fictional livestream, a viewer says a product stopped working after three months and that they were sent between support teams. Both colleagues can log the case and check the warranty status. Neither can authorise compensation.

One part of the response is to understand what the fault has disrupted and what the viewer hopes will happen next. Another is to check the purchase date, model and support record. Either colleague can gather both kinds of information.

Confirm what the team can do and who will follow up. If the outcome is still uncertain, say which details need checking. Either person can respond with care while sticking to what is known.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: a cousin asks about three cameras

In a fictional example, a cousin who wants to start making videos shares the same budget, list of three cameras and specification sheet with two relatives. Both have the same information about how the camera will be used.

One consideration is how each option would fit the cousin’s needs, including weight, ease of use and access to repairs. Another is whether each camera meets the same recording requirements, such as stabilisation or the length of a continuous clip. Either person can weigh both.

A camera that meets the recording requirements may be awkward to carry. A light camera may fall short of the quality or recording time the cousin needs. Those are trade-offs to evaluate using the same criteria.

If a comparison is possible, have the cousin film the same short scene with two candidates. The test can reveal handling and usability differences. It does not reveal either relative’s type.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: when a livestream loses its connection

In a fictional livestream, the connection drops forty minutes in. Both colleagues can see the same status information and use the same approved alert and backup options. Neither yet knows when the stream will return.

One useful contribution is an audience update stating what is known and when the team will update them again. Another is checking the approved backup and recording what is still uncertain. Either colleague can take either task if they have authority.

If the team knows the next update time, it can share that without promising when service will resume. The choice to post or check the backup depends on the information and assignments, so it cannot identify a type.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two colleagues on a live production team who both check a product record before answering a question. A shared preference for concrete evidence could fit that choice, and so could a team procedure. The action alone gives little evidence about either type.

Both profiles have S, the preference for concrete details and experience. Type dynamics gives ESFJ introverted Sensing (Si) and ISTP extraverted Sensing (Se) as auxiliary functions. Neither limits a person to what is visible right now.

E/I concerns where attention goes. T/F concerns what carries weight in a decision. J/P concerns how much to settle in the outside world. A person can discuss a question with others, apply a rule consistently and still keep more than one option open.

Several considerations can matter in one response. A team might make sure a claim is backed by evidence and answer a viewer’s concern directly. Both people can give weight to those considerations.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: responding to a question about sponsorship

In a fictional livestream, a viewer asks whether the team was paid to praise a product. Both colleagues have the same confirmed information about the sponsorship and test results. Both can share the same approved facts and refer questions they cannot answer.

One reason to include more explanation is to address the viewer’s concern about trust. Another is to make sure the same evidence standard applies to every claim about the review. These illustrate the effects on people and the use of consistent criteria. Either colleague can consider both.

Distinguish what is known about the commercial arrangement from what the product test actually showed. A statement about sponsorship does not establish performance. A test result does not explain the sponsorship.

Either person might check a record or acknowledge the question first. The deadline, assignment and information available can explain that order.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: why Fe and Ti trade places

ESFJ’s J points to an outward-facing judging function, Fe, and E makes it dominant. ISTP’s P points to an outward-facing perceiving function, Se. Because ISTP is introverted, Se supports its inward-facing dominant judging function, Ti.

Both stacks have the same judging pair, Fe and Ti, with their dominant and inferior positions swapped. Their auxiliary perceiving functions are Si and Se, respectively. The model describes how these preferences fit together. It does not rank people’s reasoning, interpersonal skills or technical ability.

The Foundation lists Ne or Ni as possible tertiary Intuition for both types. This article uses Ne for ESFJ and Ni for ISTP. A different tertiary convention can change whether an Intuition label is shared, while the Fe/Ti swap still holds. Read the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ISTP profile](/en/personality/istp) for their four preferences.

sections.title: ESFJ and ISTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
The following fictional examples show how people might handle the same information. Either type can do any of the tasks. Assign work according to experience, access, authority and availability.

Before the stream, agree on who can answer a question, which facts can be shared and who will follow up if an answer is unavailable.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: an upset viewer reports a faulty product

In a fictional livestream, a viewer says a product stopped working after three months and that they were sent between support teams. Both colleagues can log the case and check the warranty status. Neither can authorise compensation.

One part of the response is to understand what the fault has disrupted and what the viewer hopes will happen next. Another is to check the purchase date, model and support record. Either colleague can gather both kinds of information.

Confirm what the team can do and who will follow up. If the outcome is still uncertain, say which details need checking. Either person can respond with care while sticking to what is known.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: a cousin asks about three cameras

In a fictional example, a cousin who wants to start making videos shares the same budget, list of three cameras and specification sheet with two relatives. Both have the same information about how the camera will be used.

One consideration is how each option would fit the cousin’s needs, including weight, ease of use and access to repairs. Another is whether each camera meets the same recording requirements, such as stabilisation or the length of a continuous clip. Either person can weigh both.

A camera that meets the recording requirements may be awkward to carry. A light camera may fall short of the quality or recording time the cousin needs. Those are trade-offs to evaluate using the same criteria.

If a comparison is possible, have the cousin film the same short scene with two candidates. The test can reveal handling and usability differences. It does not reveal either relative’s type.

### ### ESFJ and ISTP: when a livestream loses its connection

In a fictional livestream, the connection drops forty minutes in. Both colleagues can see the same status information and use the same approved alert and backup options. Neither yet knows when the stream will return.

One useful contribution is an audience update stating what is known and when the team will update them again. Another is checking the approved backup and recording what is still uncertain. Either colleague can take either task if they have authority.

If the team knows the next update time, it can share that without promising when service will resume. The choice to post or check the backup depends on the information and assignments, so it cannot identify a type.
